sections.text: In Rust, everything inside a module is private by default. Private means: only code in that module, and in the modules nested inside it, can use the item. To let the outside world in, you add pub.

main can call reveal and peek because they are pub. It cannot call secret directly: writing outer::secret() in main fails with E0603, function secret is private. The rule of thumb: children can see their parents' private items, but parents and neighbours can't see a child's private items. This lets a module hide its inner workings.

pub also works on structs, but a struct has two levels. pub struct makes the type public. Each field is still private unless it has its own pub. So a module can keep a field private and let outsiders change it only through methods.

owner is public, so main can read it. balance is private, so main can only use deposit and balance(). Writing acc.balance from main would fail with E0616: field balance of struct Account is private. Notice that Account::new is also needed: main can't build Account { ... } itself, because it can't name the private field. Enums are different. If an enum is pub, all of its variants are public automatically.
Writing long paths gets tiring. The use keyword brings a name into scope so you can use the short form. use only affects the module it is written in, so a nested module needs its own use lines.

There is a common habit: bring in types directly (use std::collections::HashMap;), but bring in the parent module for functions (use zoo::show, then show::line). That way a call like show::line shows where the function comes from. Braces group names from one path: use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};. A * (use std::collections::*;) imports everything public, but hides where names come from, so it is rare.
The word as gives an imported item a new name. std::fmt::Result and std::io::Result are two different types with the same name, so as keeps them apart:

Think of a module as a room with a front desk. Anything marked pub is on the desk for visitors. Everything else stays in the back room. use is like writing a short nickname on a sticky note so you don't have to say the full address every time. as lets you pick the nickname.

use is the same idea as import in Python or JavaScript, and as is like import ... as. The big difference is the default: in Rust the author of a module decides what to share with pub. There are finer levels too. pub(crate) means visible anywhere inside this crate but not to other crates; pub(super) means visible to the parent module. pub use re-exports a name, so users of your library see a tidier path. These come into play once you write libraries.

exercise.prompt: Make three changes. 1) Add a method pub fn withdraw(&mut self, amount: i64) to Account that subtracts the amount from the balance. 2) Add the line use bank::Account; above main and write Account::new("Ada") instead of bank::Account::new("Ada"). 3) In main, call acc.withdraw(10) right after the deposit. It should print: Ada: 30

quiz.question: If you write an item in a module with no pub, who can use it?
options: Only code in that exact module, not in modules nested inside it
Every module in the program, but only inside the same file
Only code in that module and in the modules nested inside it

quiz.question: A module has pub struct Account { pub owner: String, balance: i64 }. What can code outside the module do with an Account value?
options: It can read owner, but cannot touch balance directly
It can read and change both fields, since the struct is pub
It can read balance, but cannot touch owner directly

quiz.question: What does the as in use std::io::Result as IoResult; do?
options: Makes the imported item public to other modules
Gives the imported item a new local name
Converts the imported type into a different type
